facts.statement: The genus Phoeniconotius was described by Miller in 1963.
The only recognized species within the genus is Phoeniconotius eyrensis.
This extinct flamingo genus lived in Australia during the late Oligocene to the early Miocene.
facts.quote: Phoeniconotius is an extinct genus of flamingo that lived in Australia from the late Oligocene to the early Miocene.

facts.statement: Fossils of Phoeniconotius were found in the Etadunna Formation mudstone on the western shore of Lake Palankarinna in Australia's Lake Eyre basin.
facts.quote: The fossils of Phoeniconotius have been discovered in the Lake Eyre basin of Australia, specifically a layer of mudstone belonging to the Etadunna Formation on the western shore of Lake Palankarinna.

facts.statement: Phoeniconotius is distinguished from modern flamingos by a clear scar for the first metatarsal attachment, whereas modern flamingos have a reduced or missing hallux.
facts.quote: This clearly separates Phoeniconotius from today's flamingos, in which the hallux is either reduced past the point of leaving visible attachment points on the tarsometatarsus or missing entirely.

facts.statement: The foot of Phoeniconotius is broader and deeper than that of the largest sampled male greater flamingo.
facts.quote: Both in breadth and depth the foot of Phoeniconotius exceeds that of the largest male greater flamingo sampled by the paper.

facts.statement: The robust phalanges and well-developed first toe of Phoeniconotius suggest it was more like a terrestrial wader, such as a stork or crane, rather than an aquatic flamingo.
facts.quote: This is further supported by the robust phalanges and the seemingly well developed first toe, which is reduced in flamingos but well developed in less aquatic wading birds like storks and cranes.

facts.statement: Phoeniconotius belongs to the family Phoenicopteridae.

rejected.statement: Phoeniconotius was a robust flamingo possessing bones more massive than those of the modern greater flamingo.
rejected.quote: Phoeniconotius was a robust flamingo with bones more massive than those of the modern greater flamingo.
